title: Classes & Objects
summary: The blueprint and the built thing. Learn how classes define shape and objects hold state, one instance at a time.

blocks.markdown:
A **class** is a blueprint — it defines what data and behavior something has, but holds no data itself. An **object** is one built instance of that blueprint, with its own real values.

- One class, many objects — each with its own state.
- Classes group **attributes** (data) and **methods** (behavior) together.
- This bundling is the starting point for all of OOP.

blocks.subTitle: Blueprint vs instance
blocks.markdown:
The classic analogy.

| Concept | Real-world parallel |
|---|---|
| Class | House blueprint |
| Object | An actual built house |
| Attribute | Number of rooms |

The blueprint is drawn once; you can build many houses from it, each standing on its own.

A **class** exists once in your code, at compile or definition time. An **object** exists at runtime — created when the program actually needs one.

- Defining `class Car` creates no car; it only describes what a car has.
- Writing `myCar = new Car()` creates a real object in memory.
- Many objects can come from the same class, each independent of the others.

A class bundles two kinds of members.

- **Attributes** (also called fields or properties) — the data an object holds, its **state**. Example: a car's `speed` and `fuelLevel`.
- **Methods** — the actions an object can perform, its **behavior**. Example: `accelerate()`, `refuel()`.

Methods usually read or change the object's own attributes.

blocks.subTitle: State vs behavior
blocks.markdown:
**State** is what an object currently *is* — the values of its attributes at a moment in time. **Behavior** is what it can *do* — its methods.

- Two `Car` objects share the same behavior (both can `accelerate()`) but usually differ in state (different `speed`).
- State changes over time; behavior is fixed by the class.

**Instantiation** is the act of creating an object from a class. It's done through a **constructor** — a special method that runs once, when the object is created, to set up its initial state.

- The constructor usually takes parameters and assigns them to attributes.
- If you don't write one, most languages supply a default (empty) constructor.
- Every object goes through construction before it can be used.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: defining a class
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Car:
    // attributes (state)
    make
    speed

    // constructor — runs on creation
    constructor(make):
        this.make = make
        this.speed = 0

    // methods (behavior)
    method accelerate(amount):
        this.speed = this.speed + amount

    method describe():
        print(this.make + " at " + this.speed + " km/h")
```

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: creating objects
blocks.markdown:
```text
// instantiation — each call builds a separate object
myCar = new Car("Tesla")
yourCar = new Car("Honda")

myCar.accelerate(40)
yourCar.accelerate(10)

myCar.describe()    // Tesla at 40 km/h
yourCar.describe()  // Honda at 10 km/h
```

Same class, same methods — but each object's state moves independently.

Inside a method, **`this`** (called `self` in some languages) refers to the specific object the method was called on. It's how a method reaches its own attributes.

- `this.speed` means "the `speed` of whichever object is running right now."
- Without it, `accelerate()` couldn't tell your car's speed from mine.
- It's set automatically by the language when a method is called.

**Instance members** belong to one object — each object has its own copy. **Static** (or class) members belong to the class itself, shared by every object.

- `speed` is per-car — instance data.
- A `totalCarsBuilt` counter shared across all cars is **static** — one copy, updated by every constructor call.
- Static methods can't use `this` — there's no single object to refer to.

blocks.subTitle: Quick contrast
blocks.markdown:
| Member | Belongs to | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Instance | Each object | `myCar.speed` |
| Static | The class | `Car.totalCarsBuilt` |

Use static for things true of the class as a whole — counters, constants, factory helpers.

Every object moves through a short lifecycle.

- **Created** — the constructor runs, memory is allocated, initial state is set.
- **Used** — methods are called, attributes change, the object does its job.
- **Destroyed** — once nothing refers to it, it's cleaned up. Languages like Java/Python do this automatically via **garbage collection**; C++ requires manual cleanup.

You rarely manage this by hand in garbage-collected languages.

Common mix-ups:

- **"Class and object are the same thing."** No — one is the definition, the other is a live instance built from it.
- **Confusing static with instance.** A static counter shared by mistake as instance data causes every object to silently share one value.
- **Skipping the constructor.** Leaving attributes unset until "later" invites bugs from objects used before they're ready.

blocks.subTitle: Class vs object
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between a class and an object?**

A class is a blueprint — it defines attributes and methods but holds no actual data. An object is a concrete instance of a class, with its own real values for those attributes. One class can produce many independent objects.

blocks.subTitle: What is a constructor
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a constructor and when does it run?**

A constructor is a special method that runs exactly once, at the moment an object is created, to set up its initial state. It typically takes parameters and assigns them to the new object's attributes before anything else can use it.

blocks.subTitle: Instance vs static members
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between instance and static members?**

Instance members belong to a single object — each object gets its own copy (e.g. a car's `speed`). Static members belong to the class itself and are shared by every object (e.g. a `totalCarsBuilt` counter). Static methods can't reference `this` because they aren't tied to one object.

blocks.subTitle: What does this/self refer to
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What does `this` (or `self`) refer to inside a method?**

It refers to the specific object the method is currently running on. It's how a method reaches that object's own attributes rather than some other object's — `this.speed` always means "my speed," set automatically by the language at call time.
